hz3_officials.topic: Would Hezbollah exist? Israeli officials' own words

claims.text: Ehud Barak, 2006, as quoted: 'When we entered Lebanon, there was no Hezbollah. We were accepted by perfumed rice and flowers by the Shi'a in the south.' and 'It was our presence there that created Hezbollah.' The Statesman column gives no outlet; Wikipedia's Hezbollah article dates the remarks to 2006. Original outlet (commonly said to be Newsweek) not confirmed.

Rabin (defence minister), Feb 1985: if Israel replaced PLO terrorism with Shiite terrorism 'we have done the worst (thing) in our struggle against terrorism'; 'the Shiites have the potential for a kind of terrorism that we have not yet experienced.'; on the security zone: 'If there is a problem we will bomb them, we'll shell them.'

CSM, 11 March 1985: Shiites had 'sworn to drive the Israelis out of Lebanon'; Rabin reportedly feared Shiite 'hatred' of Israel more than Palestinian attacks; a Western analyst: no way the Shiites would 'just going to stop at the border' after withdrawal.

CSM, 21 June 1985: more than 1,000 Shiites, most held at the Ansar camp, were taken across the border into Israel during the April 1985 withdrawal; the ICRC and the US condemned it as a violation of the Geneva Convention.
Rabin, 22 Sept 1986 (Antenne 2): wanted to help the SLA 'with our firepower to permanently break any future offensive' and cause 'such losses' that the will to attack is reduced.

claims.text: Norton, July 2006: 'Hezbollah didn't exist in the early 1980s and was in effect created by the Israeli occupation of Lebanon and by Iran'; 'the Israeli presence in Lebanon basically created Hezbollah'; 'Iran was attempting to extend its revolutionary goals to places like Lebanon'.

Teague's review of Norton: radicalisation 'did not take place in a vacuum' (al-Sadr's 1978 disappearance, Iran's revolution, Israel's invasion); Norton quotes Barak and Rabin conceding the occupation 'provided the context in which Hezbollah was created'; Norton stresses Iraq, 'where many of Hezbollah's leading intellectuals originated', and a 'directive from Iraq to infiltrate an increasingly secular Amal'; Hezbollah 'had not fully cohered until about 1984'.

Divine's review: Norton argues the 'profoundly destructive Israeli invasion of Lebanon in 1982' weakened the PLO but helped create 'a far more formidable' adversary, Hezbollah, alongside growing Shia political awareness.

hz3_before.topic: Shia mobilisation and Islamist networks before 1982

claims.text: Musa al-Sadr left Najaf for Tyre in late 1959; first head of the Supreme Islamic Shia Council 1969; founded the Movement of the Disinherited with Hussein el-Husseini in 1974; went to Libya 25 Aug 1978 at Gaddafi's invitation, last seen 31 Aug 1978.

Amal (Movement of the Deprived) founded 6 July 1974; military wing formed January 1975; Shia community 'the poorest and most neglected by the Lebanese government'; mobilisation grew after al-Sadr's disappearance, the 1978 conflict and the 1979 revolution; in summer 1982 deputy Husayn al-Musawi broke away to form Islamic Amal.

Dawa party founded in Iraq (dates 1957 to late 1960s; Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr leading figure); Iran played a key role 'especially its Lebanese branch which later became Hezbollah'; Hezbollah co-founders Abbas al-Musawi and Mohammad Yazbek listed as Dawa members; 12 Dec 1983 Kuwait bombings (US and French embassies, airport, refinery), 17 suspects arrested, mostly Dawa members, presented as punishment for aiding Iraq.

Fadlallah studied 21 years in Najaf, returned to Lebanon 1966; called Hezbollah's 'spiritual mentor' in media, a status he and the group denied; Qassem said Hezbollah began as factions of Islamic movements inspired by Fadlallah.

Shapira (ITIC): 'The decision to establish Hezbollah was made in Tehran three years before Israel invaded Lebanon'; the invasion was a catalyst, not the cause; quotes Naim Qassem: 'the Israeli invasion of Lebanon was not the reason Hezbollah was founded.'

Shapira: Khomeini's Council of the Islamic Revolution decided to export the revolution; Montazeri built a network supporting movements in the Hijaz, Bahrain, Kuwait and Lebanon; Ali Akbar Mohtashami became ambassador in Damascus in August 1981, founded Hezbollah from the embassy as an alternative to Amal and chaired its Council of Lebanon until 1986; the IRGC built its military force at the Sheikh Abdallah barracks (renamed Imam Ali) near Baalbek.

Shapira: Amal, founded in 1974 by Musa al-Sadr and Mostafa Chamran, was seen in Tehran as secular; it rejected velayat-e faqih and stayed loyal to the Lebanese state. ITIC also quotes Barak, undated: 'When we entered Lebanon Hezbollah didn't exist, we were welcomed with flowers and rice.'

Wikipedia: Hezbollah was backed initially by about 1,500 IRGC instructors who arrived with Syrian permission and trained fighters in the Bekaa; it treats the 8 June 1982 Khalde ambush (two days after the invasion) as the founding myth of its military wing; its 16 Feb 1985 manifesto (read by Ibrahim al-Amin) targeted 'the Israeli occupation of Southern Lebanon', rejected Israel's existence, and pledged allegiance to Iran's supreme leader under wilayat al-faqih.

hz3_itic_shapira.label: Brig. Gen. (res.) Dr. Shimon Shapira, 'The Birth of Hezbollah', Meir Amit Intelligence and Terrorism Information Center (IICC Perspectives), 19 January 2023 (first published September 2022)
